cards.explanation_correct: Threat intelligence (TI/CTI) transforms raw threat data into actionable knowledge. The three levels serve different purposes and audiences: (1) STRATEGIC TI — answers 'WHO is attacking and WHY?' It's about understanding the threat landscape at a high level: which sectors are being targeted, what motivations drive attacks (financial, espionage, disruption), emerging trends (AI-powered phishing, supply chain attacks), and geopolitical context. Format: reports, briefings, white papers. Sources: government advisories (CISA, NCSC), industry ISACs (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers), vendor research reports (Mandiant, CrowdStrike). Value: helps executives allocate budget ('we need more healthcare-sector threat intel because APTs are targeting us'), prioritize initiatives, and understand risk in business terms. Time horizon: months to years. (2) OPERATIONAL TI — answers 'HOW are they attacking?' It focuses on specific campaigns and TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures). TTPs describe the attacker's methods mapped to frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK. Example: 'This campaign uses spear phishing → credential harvesting → VPN access → Cobalt Strike → lateral movement → data exfiltration via DNS.' Format: campaign reports, TTP mappings, YARA rules. Value: helps IR teams prepare for specific attack patterns, build detection content (SIEM rules, EDR queries), and conduct threat hunting. Time horizon: weeks to months. (3) TACTICAL TI (IOC-level) — answers 'WHAT specific indicators should I block/detect?' IOCs (Indicators of Compromise): malicious IPs, domains, URLs, file hashes, email sender addresses. Format: STIX/TAXII feeds, CSV lists, API integrations. Value: directly ingestible into security tools (firewall blocklists, SIEM correlation rules, EDR deny lists). Challenge: IOCs have short lifespans — attackers rotate IPs/domains quickly (sometimes within hours). Tactical TI is high-volume but low-durability. The intelligence pyramid: TTPs (top, most durable, hardest to change) > Tools > Network artifacts > Host artifacts > Domain names > IP addresses > Hash values (bottom, least durable, easiest to change). Investing in TTP-level intelligence (operational) provides longer-lasting defensive value than IOC-level (tactical).
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Threat intelligence is NOT just IP blocklists — that's only tactical TI (the lowest level). It's a common misconception because many 'threat intel' vendors sell IOC feeds and call it 'threat intelligence.' TI is NOT the same as threat hunting — threat hunting is the ACTIVITY of proactively searching for threats in your network, often USING threat intelligence as input. TI is the INPUT; hunting is the ACTION. TI is NOT government-only — private sector threat intelligence is a massive industry (Mandiant, CrowdStrike, Recorded Future, Anomali). ISACs (FS-ISAC for financial, H-ISAC for healthcare) facilitate private-sector intel sharing. The common mistakes: (a) Confusing the three levels and serving tactical IOCs to executives (they don't care about IPs, they care about business risk) or serving strategic reports to SOC analysts (they can't block a 'trend'). (b) Over-investing in tactical TI (IOC feeds) while neglecting operational TI (TTPs) — IOCs expire quickly but TTPs persist. (c) Treating TI as a product to buy rather than a process to integrate — a feed you don't operationalize (ingest, correlate, act on) is useless. The key insight: effective TI programs deliver the RIGHT level of intelligence to the RIGHT audience at the RIGHT time.

cards.question_text: Your organization's SIEM alerts on a workstation making DNS queries to a domain flagged in a threat intelligence feed. The TI report links this domain to APT41 (a Chinese state-sponsored group targeting healthcare and technology sectors). Your company is a biotech research firm. Describe your incident response process, what artifacts to collect, and how to determine if this is a true positive or a false positive. How do you avoid alert fatigue from TI feeds?
choices: Response process: (1) TRIAGE — check if the DNS query is from the TI feed (true positive indicator) or a benign collision (same domain used by legitimate service). Verify the TI feed's confidence rating. (2) CONTAIN — isolate the workstation from the network (EDR network containment or VLAN quarantine) to prevent potential C2 communication while preserving evidence. (3) COLLECT — preserve volatile evidence first: RAM dump (for running processes, injected code), network connections (netstat, EDR network timeline), DNS logs, process tree (what process made the query?), file system timeline (recently created/modified files), registry changes, scheduled tasks, and the original weaponized document/email if identifiable. (4) ANALYZE — map findings to MITRE ATT&CK (which TTPs are present?), compare to APT41's known TTPs from the TI report, check for lateral movement indicators (SMB connections, RDP logins, credential access). (5) SCOPE — search all systems for the same indicators (domain, related IPs, file hashes, mutexes) to determine blast radius. (6) False positive indicators: the domain is also used by a legitimate CDN/ad network (benign collision), the query was from a browser visiting a compromised site (drive-by, not targeted), or the TI feed has low confidence/stale data. (7) Avoid alert fatigue: tune TI feeds (remove low-confidence/noisy indicators), add context to alerts (asset criticality, user role, historical baseline), correlate multiple signals (don't alert on a single DNS query — correlate with process behavior, file creation, network connections), and use risk scoring (score each indicator by confidence + asset criticality + TTP match)
Immediately wipe and reinstall the workstation — there's no time for analysis when an APT is involved
Ignore the alert — threat intelligence feeds have too many false positives to be useful
Only check if the workstation's antivirus flagged anything — if AV is clean, there's no compromise

cards.explanation_correct: This scenario combines threat intelligence, incident response, and alert management. The IR process follows NIST SP 800-61 (Preparation → Detection & Analysis → Containment, Eradication & Recovery → Post-Incident Activity). Key points: (1) TRIAGE is critical because TI-based alerts have high false positive rates — domains can be dual-use (legitimate CDN compromised and used for C2), TI feeds can be stale (domain was malicious 6 months ago, now registered by a legitimate company), or the query could be passive (browser pre-fetch, DNS prefetching by a browser extension). Verify: TI feed confidence rating (high/medium/low), date of last update, whether the domain is on multiple independent feeds (corroboration), and passive DNS history (who else has queried this domain?). (2) CONTAIN but DON'T DESTROY — a common mistake is wiping the machine immediately, which destroys evidence needed for attribution and scoping. Isolate (network containment) while preserving the running system for forensic analysis. EDR tools (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) can contain a host with one click while maintaining forensic access. (3) EVIDENCE COLLECTION order (volatility principle — collect most volatile first): RAM (running processes, injected code, network connections, decryption keys in memory) → network state (active connections, listening ports) → process tree → disk (files, registry, logs). Tools: Velociraptor, KAPE, FTK Imager, EDR's built-in forensic tools. (4) ANALYSIS using MITRE ATT&CK: map observed behaviors to known techniques. APT41 TTPs include: spear phishing with weaponized Office docs (T1566.001), PowerShell execution (T1059.001), credential dumping with Mimikatz (T1003.001), lateral movement via RDP/WMI (T1021.001/T1047), Cobalt Strike or PlugX as C2 framework (T1071). If the workstation shows multiple matching TTPs, confidence in true positive increases dramatically. (5) SCOPING: use EDR search across all endpoints for the same indicators — the compromised workstation may be patient zero, or it may be one of many already compromised. (6) ALERT FATIGUE is the #1 problem with TI integration. Solutions: (a) FEED QUALITY over quantity — one high-confidence curated feed beats ten noisy ones. (b) CONTEXTUAL ALERTING — a TI hit on a domain controller is critical; the same hit on a guest network laptop is low priority. (c) CORRELATION — don't alert on a single indicator; correlate TI hits with other signals (new process creation, network connection to new IP, file write) before alerting. (d) RISK SCORING — assign each alert a score based on: TI confidence × asset criticality × TTP alignment × behavioral corroboration. Only page analysts for high-risk scores. (e) FEEDBACK LOOP — analysts mark alerts as true/false positive; this feedback tunes future alerting. The biotech context matters — APT41 actively targets biotech/pharma for intellectual property theft. A TI hit matching APT41 against a biotech firm has higher prior probability of being a true positive than the same hit against a random small business. Context-aware threat intelligence is more valuable than context-free IOC matching.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Immediately wiping the workstation is the WORST response — it destroys all forensic evidence (RAM contents, running processes, registry modifications, log files). Without evidence, you can't determine: how the attacker got in (to prevent re-entry), what data they accessed (for breach notification), whether they moved laterally (other compromised systems), or attribute the attack. Wiping treats the symptom (one infected machine) without understanding the disease (the full compromise). Ignoring all TI alerts is equally dangerous — while false positives are common, dismissing ALL alerts means missing the true positives that indicate active compromise. TI feeds require TUNING, not abandonment. Relying only on AV is insufficient — APTs use custom malware that signature-based AV doesn't detect (as seen in the RAT scenario). The common mistakes: (a) Treating IR as 'wipe and restore' instead of 'investigate, scope, and remediate' — wiping without scoping often leaves other compromised systems undiscovered. (b) Binary alert handling (alert on everything vs. ignore everything) instead of risk-based triage. (c) Not using MITRE ATT&CK for analysis — without TTP mapping, you can't distinguish a targeted APT attack from opportunistic malware. (d) Not collecting RAM/volatile evidence — disk-only forensics misses in-memory malware, injected code, and active network connections. The key lesson: incident response is a structured investigative process, not a 'nuke and pave' reflex. Contain, preserve, analyze, scope, THEN remediate.
